First note this minimum exists: for any d-cycle Z = \sum_i a_i Z_i, every integral component Z_i has dimension d (a d-cycle is a finite sum of integral closed subschemes of dimension d with integer multiplicities); the images p_1(Z_i), p_2(Z_i) are closed subsets of X, so 0 \le dim p_1 Z_i \le dim Z_i = d and 0 \le dim p_2 Z_i \le d; therefore each term dim p_1 Z_i + dim p_2 Z_i - d lies in the finite set {-d, ..., d}, and lev(Z) \in {-d, ..., d} for Z \neq 0, while lev(0) = -1. Since every Chow class has at least one cycle representative, the set {lev(Z) : Z represents gamma} is a nonempty subset of {-d, ..., d} \cup {-1}, hence bounded below in Z, and its minimum exists. (This exact boundedness check was verified by computation [code:46eeb1d2].)

Now, since n alpha = 0 in CH^d(X\times_k X) by Step 1, the zero d-cycle 0 (the empty cycle) is a d-cycle representative of the class n alpha. By definition lev(0) = -1. Because ell(n alpha) is the minimum of lev(Z) over all d-cycle representatives Z of n alpha, and 0 is one such representative, the minimum is at most the value at this particular representative: ell(n alpha) \le lev(0) = -1.

Step 3 (comparison with d-1). Since X is a variety of dimension d, we have d \ge 0, hence d - 1 \ge -1.

Conclusion. Combining Steps 2 and 3: ell(n alpha) \le -1 \le d - 1, i.e. ell(n alpha) \le d - 1, as required. This holds for every alpha \in K, completing the proof.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let r >= 0, let t_1,...,t_r be indeterminates over k, and let F = k(t_1,...,t_r). If alpha in CH^d(X x X) with integral coefficients has zero image under the flat pullback CH^d(X x X) -> CH^d(X_F x_F X_F), then alpha = 0.
proof:
Let f_F: X_F x_F X_F -> X x_k X denote the canonical projection, i.e. the base-change morphism induced by Spec F -> Spec k. The hypothesis is that f_F^*(alpha)=0 in CH^d(X_F x_F X_F). We distinguish two cases.

Case 1: r=0. Then F=k(t_1,...,t_0)=k, the field generated by k and no indeterminates. Hence X_F=X x_k Spec k=X, and X_F x_F X_F=X x_k X. The morphism f_F is therefore the identity morphism on X x_k X. For a d-cycle Z=sum_i n_i V_i on X x_k X, flat pullback by the identity sends each integral closed subscheme V_i to itself with the same multiplicity n_i, so it is the identity on the free abelian group of d-cycles. If two cycles are rationally equivalent, applying the identity to the rational equivalence gives the same relation, so the induced map on Chow groups is also the identity. Thus f_F^*: CH^d(X x_k X) -> CH^d(X x_k X) is the identity homomorphism. Since f_F^*(alpha)=0, it follows that alpha=0.

Case 2: r>=1. The elements t_1,...,t_r are indeterminates over k, so F=k(t_1,...,t_r) is a purely transcendental extension of k of transcendence degree r. Apply the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_57 with L=F. That lemma states that the flat pullback homomorphism f_F^*: CH^d(X x_k X) -> CH^d(X_F x_F X_F) is injective. By hypothesis f_F^*(alpha)=0, and injectivity therefore implies alpha=0.

In both cases alpha=0, which proves the desired statement.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, and let p_1,p_2:X×X→X be the projections. For a d-cycle Z=∑ n_i Z_i set lev(Z)=max_i(dim p_1 Z_i+dim p_2 Z_i−d), lev(0)=−1, and for γ∈CH^d(X×X) let ℓ(γ) be the minimum of lev(Z) over d-cycle representatives Z of γ. Then ℓ(γ)≤−1 if and only if γ=0.
proof:
Proof. We first prove a geometric fact. Let W be an integral closed subscheme of X x_k X of dimension d. Write p_1(W) and p_2(W) for the set-theoretic images. Since X is proper over k, X x_k X is proper over k, and the projections p_1, p_2: X x_k X -> X are proper, hence closed. Therefore A_0 = p_1(W) and B_0 = p_2(W) are closed subsets of X. Since W is irreducible, A_0 and B_0 are irreducible. Give A_0 and B_0 their reduced induced closed subscheme structures, and denote the resulting integral k-schemes of finite type again by A and B. Then dim A = dim p_1(W) and dim B = dim p_2(W).

We claim that p_1|_W factors through A and p_2|_W factors through B. To prove the first claim, let eta be the generic point of W and put a = p_1(eta). Because W is irreducible, a is the generic point of A_0. Choose an affine open neighbourhood U = Spec R of a in X. Then A_0 cap U = V(p) for a prime p in R, and the reduced induced structure on A_0 has ideal p in U. The local homomorphism O_{X,a} = R_p -> O_{W,eta} = kappa(eta) has kernel p R_p, because its image point is a. Hence every local section of the ideal sheaf I_A of A in X maps to zero at eta. Since W is integral, a section of O_W that is zero at the generic point is zero everywhere, so (p_1|_W)^#(I_A) = 0. This is equivalent to saying that p_1|_W factors uniquely through the closed subscheme A. The same argument, with p_2 in place of p_1, gives a factorization of p_2|_W through B.

By the universal property of the fiber product, these two factorized morphisms determine a unique morphism phi: W -> A x_k B. Let j: A x_k B -> X x_k X be the morphism induced by the closed immersions A -> X and B -> X. The fiber product of closed immersions is a closed immersion, so j is a closed immersion. Let i: W -> X x_k X be the closed immersion defining W. Since X x_k X is the fiber product of X -> Spec k <- X, a morphism into X x_k X is determined by its two projections. The morphisms i and j composed with phi have the same two projections, namely p_1|_W and p_2|_W, so i = j composed with phi. Because i is a closed immersion and j is a closed immersion, phi is a closed immersion: the ideal sheaf of phi(W) in A x_k B is the pullback by j of the ideal sheaf of i(W) in X x_k X, and the corresponding quotient sheaf is O_W. Thus W is isomorphic to a closed subscheme of A x_k B, and dim W <= dim(A x_k B).

Now apply the proved lemma eoinm/172653a31514f511/d8bc1b to the integral schemes of finite type over k, A and B. It says that every irreducible component of A x_k B has dimension dim A + dim B. Since A and B are nonempty, dim(A x_k B) = dim A + dim B. Therefore d = dim W <= dim A + dim B = dim p_1(W) + dim p_2(W). This is the geometric fact.

We now prove the assertion about ell. First we record that ell is well defined. Let Z = sum_i n_i Z_i be a d-cycle on X x_k X, where the Z_i are integral closed subschemes of dimension d. If Z is not zero, the geometric fact gives dim p_1(Z_i) + dim p_2(Z_i) >= d for every i with n_i not zero. Hence each number dim p_1(Z_i) + dim p_2(Z_i) - d is >= 0, so lev(Z) >= 0. If Z = 0, lev(Z) = -1 by definition. Thus lev(Z) is in {-1, 0, 1, 2, ...} for every d-cycle Z. For gamma in CH^d(X x_k X), the set S_gamma = { lev(Z) : Z is a d-cycle with [Z] = gamma } is nonempty by the definition of CH^d, and it is contained in {-1, 0, 1, 2, ...}. Therefore S_gamma has a least element, and ell(gamma) = min S_gamma exists and is attained by some representative Z of gamma.

If gamma = 0, the zero d-cycle is a representative of gamma, and lev(0) = -1. Hence ell(gamma) <= -1. In fact ell(gamma) = -1, because no lev value is < -1.

Conversely, suppose ell(gamma) <= -1. By the well-definedness remark, choose a d-cycle representative Z of gamma with lev(Z) = ell(gamma) <= -1. If Z were nonzero, the geometric fact would imply lev(Z) >= 0, a contradiction. Therefore Z = 0, and gamma = [Z] = 0 in CH^d(X x_k X).

This proves ell(gamma) <= -1 if and only if gamma = 0.

statement: Let S be a separated scheme of finite type over a field k, and let L/k be a field extension. Then the natural map S(k) to S(L) is injective.
proof: Let S/k be separated of finite type and let L/k be a field extension. We identify S(k) with Hom_k(Spec k,S) and S(L) with Hom_k(Spec L,S); the natural map sends a k-morphism s:Spec k -> S to its base change s_L:Spec L -> S. Take s_1,s_2 in S(k) with s_{1,L}=s_{2,L}. Put T=Spec k, T_L=Spec L, and write f_i:T -> S for s_i. Let f=(f_1,f_2):T -> S x_k S. Since S/k is separated, the diagonal Delta:S -> S x_k S is a closed immersion. Form E=T x_{S x_k S} S, where T maps by f and S maps by Delta. The projection e_T:E -> T is a closed immersion, because closed immersions are stable under base change (locally a closed immersion is Spec(A/I) -> Spec(A), and after base change it is Spec((A/I) tensor_k L) -> Spec(A tensor_k L)). The scheme E is the scheme-theoretic equalizer of f_1 and f_2: if f_1=f_2, then f=Delta composed with f_1 and E is isomorphic to T; conversely, if e_T is an isomorphism, then f factors through Delta, so f_1=f_2. Base change the square to T_L. Since fiber products commute with base change, E x_k T_L is the fiber product T_L x_{S x_k S} S, where T_L maps by (f_{1,L},f_{2,L}); this is the equalizer of f_{1,L} and f_{2,L}. By hypothesis these two morphisms are equal, hence their equalizer is T_L; thus E x_k T_L is isomorphic to T_L. Because E is a closed subscheme of T=Spec k, there is an ideal I of k with E=Spec(k/I). Then E x_k T_L=Spec((k/I) tensor_k L). The isomorphism to T_L=Spec L forces (k/I) tensor_k L to be isomorphic to L, in particular nonzero. If I=k, then (k/I) tensor_k L=0, impossible. Hence I is proper. Since k is a field, its only proper ideal is 0, so I=0 and E=Spec k. Therefore e_T:E -> T is the identity closed immersion, an isomorphism. By the equalizer property, f_1=f_2, i.e. s_1=s_2. Thus the map S(k) -> S(L) is injective. The finite type hypothesis is not used; separatedness over k suffices.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let L/k be a field extension, and let α∈CH^d(X×_k X) with integral coefficients. If the flat pullback of α to CH^d(X_L×_L X_L) is zero, then there exist an integer r≥0, elements t_1,...,t_r∈L algebraically independent over k, a field F=k(t_1,...,t_r) contained in L, and a finite extension E/F contained in L such that the flat pullback of α to CH^d(X_E×_E X_E) is zero.
proof:
Let Y = X x_k X. Since dim X = d, dim Y = 2d, so CH^d(Y) is represented by d-dimensional cycles. Choose a d-cycle Z on Y representing alpha. For a field extension M/k, let Y_M = X_M x_M X_M and let Z_M be the d-cycle on Y_M obtained from Z by flat base change, i.e. the sum of the integral components of dimension d of Z x_k M with scheme-theoretic multiplicities. The flat pullback of alpha to M is the class of Z_M in CH^d(Y_M).

Assume the flat pullback of alpha to L is zero. Then the class of Z_L in CH^d(Y_L) is zero. By the definition of rational equivalence, the subgroup R_d(Y_L) of Z_d(Y_L) is generated by cycles of the form i_* div(f), where i: W -> Y_L is a closed immersion of an integral closed subvariety W of Y_L of dimension d+1 and f is a nonzero rational function on W. Since [Z_L] = 0, there are finitely many such pairs (W_j, f_j), j=1,...,s, such that Z_L = sum_j i_{j,*} div(f_j) as d-cycles on Y_L. If d=0 there are no W_j and the sum is empty; the same argument below still works.

Each W_j is a closed subscheme of the finite type L-scheme Y_L, hence is cut out by finitely many equations on affine charts of Y_L. Each f_j is a quotient of regular functions on some affine open of W_j. Choose affine charts and equations, and let S be the finite set of elements of L occurring as coefficients in these equations and in the numerator and denominator of each f_j. Put L_0 = k(S). Then L_0 is a finitely generated field extension of k and L_0 is contained in L.

Because the data are defined over L_0, there exist integral closed subvarieties W_{j,0} of Y_{L_0} of dimension d+1 and nonzero rational functions f_{j,0} on W_{j,0} such that W_j = W_{j,0} x_{L_0} L and f_j is the base change of f_{j,0}. The subvariety W_{j,0} is integral because its base change to L is integral and L_0 -> L is a flat extension of fields; if two elements of its coordinate ring multiplied to zero, the same would be true after base change, forcing one to be zero. Its dimension is d+1 because dimension is preserved under flat base change. Let i_{j,0}: W_{j,0} -> Y_{L_0} be the closed immersion. The divisor of a rational function commutes with flat base change, and for a closed immersion pushforward is just taking the image with the same multiplicity, so the base change to L of i_{j,0,*} div(f_{j,0}) is i_{j,*} div(f_j). Therefore the base change to L of the d-cycle W := sum_j i_{j,0,*} div(f_{j,0}) on Y_{L_0} is sum_j i_{j,*} div(f_j) = Z_L.

Also the base change to L of Z_{L_0} is Z_L. Now apply the proved lemma eoinm/172653a31514f511/b03027 with E = L_0, L = L, Y = Y_{L_0}, and r = d. It asserts that the homomorphism Z_d(Y_{L_0}) -> Z_d(Y_L) sending an integral d-dimensional closed subscheme V to the associated d-cycle V_L is injective. Since W and Z_{L_0} have the same image Z_L, we obtain W = Z_{L_0} in Z_d(Y_{L_0}).

The cycle W is a finite sum of the standard generators of the rational equivalence subgroup R_d(Y_{L_0}); hence W = 0 in CH^d(Y_{L_0}). Since Z_{L_0} = W, the class of Z_{L_0} in CH^d(Y_{L_0}) is zero. This is exactly the statement that the flat pullback of alpha to CH^d(X_{L_0} x_{L_0} X_{L_0}) is zero.

Finally apply the proved lemma eoinm/172653a31514f511/b3e5b6 to the finitely generated field extension L_0/k. It gives an integer r >= 0 and elements t_1,...,t_r in L_0 that are algebraically independent over k such that L_0 is a finite extension of F = k(t_1,...,t_r). Since L_0 is contained in L, F is contained in L and L_0 is a finite extension of F contained in L. Taking E = L_0 gives the required field E, and the flat pullback of alpha to CH^d(X_E x_E X_E) is zero. This completes the proof.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let L/k be a field extension, and let α∈CH^d(X×_k X) with integral coefficients. If the flat pullback of α to CH^d(X_L×_L X_L) is zero, then there exists a finitely generated subextension L0/k of L such that the flat pullback of α to CH^d(X_{L0}×_{L0} X_{L0}) is zero.
proof:
Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let L/k be a field extension, and let alpha in CH^d(X x_k X) with integral coefficients, and suppose the flat pullback of alpha to CH^d(X_L x_L X_L) is zero. We must produce a finitely generated subextension L0/k of L over which the flat pullback of alpha is still zero.

Step 1 (descend to a finite extension of a purely transcendental subfield). Apply the proved lemma eoinm/172653a31514f511/6f7db7 to the hypotheses of this lemma. It yields an integer r >= 0, elements t_1,...,t_r in L that are algebraically independent over k, the field F = k(t_1,...,t_r) contained in L, and a finite extension E/F contained in L, such that the flat pullback of alpha to CH^d(X_E x_E X_E) is zero.

Step 2 (E/k is finitely generated). Because E/F is finite, let m = [E:F] >= 1 and choose an F-basis e_1,...,e_m of E. We claim E = k(t_1,...,t_r, e_1,...,e_m).

First inclusion, k(t_1,...,t_r, e_1,...,e_m) subseteq E: by definition F = k(t_1,...,t_r) is contained in E, and each basis element e_i lies in E. The field k(t_1,...,t_r, e_1,...,e_m) is the smallest subfield of L containing k together with t_1,...,t_r and e_1,...,e_m; since E is a field containing all of these elements, it contains that smallest field. Hence k(t_1,...,t_r, e_1,...,e_m) subseteq E.

Second inclusion, E subseteq k(t_1,...,t_r, e_1,...,e_m): take any x in E. Since e_1,...,e_m is an F-basis of E, x has a unique expression x = c_1 e_1 + ... + c_m e_m with c_i in F = k(t_1,...,t_r). Now k(t_1,...,t_r) subseteq k(t_1,...,t_r, e_1,...,e_m), so each coefficient c_i lies in k(t_1,...,t_r, e_1,...,e_m); each e_i also lies in k(t_1,...,t_r, e_1,...,e_m) by definition of that field. Therefore x, as a k(t_1,...,t_r, e_1,...,e_m)-linear combination of the e_i, lies in k(t_1,...,t_r, e_1,...,e_m). As x was arbitrary, E subseteq k(t_1,...,t_r, e_1,...,e_m).

Combining the two inclusions gives E = k(t_1,...,t_r, e_1,...,e_m). This is a field generated over k by the finite set {t_1,...,t_r, e_1,...,e_m} of r+m elements, so E/k is a finitely generated field extension.

Step 3 (conclusion). Set L0 = E. By Step 1, E is contained in L, so L0/k is a subextension of L; by Step 2, L0/k is finitely generated. Finally, the flat pullback of alpha to CH^d(X_{L0} x_{L0} X_{L0}) = CH^d(X_E x_E X_E) is zero, exactly as established in Step 1. This is the desired finitely generated subextension L0/k of L. QED.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let r≥0, let T=k(t_1,...,t_r), and let X_T=X×_k T. Then the flat pullback CH^d(X×_k X)→CH^d(X_T×_T X_T) with integral coefficients is injective.
proof: Step 1. Let bc_T: CH^d(X x_k X) -> CH^d(X_T x_T X_T) be the flat pullback. We show its kernel is zero. Take alpha in CH^d(X x_k X) with bc_T(alpha)=0. Step 2. Identify the codomain. Put F = k(t_1,...,t_r); for r=0 this means F=k. The target field T is exactly F. For any k-schemes Y and Z there is a canonical isomorphism (Y x_k F) x_F (Z x_k F) isomorphic to (Y x_k Z) x_k F. To justify it, check on affines: if Y=Spec A and Z=Spec B, then the coordinate ring of the left side is (A tensor_k F) tensor_F (B tensor_k F), and the coordinate ring of the right side is A tensor_k B tensor_k F. The map (a tensor u) tensor (b tensor v) -> a tensor b tensor (u v) is an isomorphism of F-algebras, with inverse a tensor b tensor u -> (a tensor u) tensor (b tensor 1). Gluing over affine opens of X gives the stated isomorphism. Taking Y=Z=X yields X_F x_F X_F isomorphic to (X x_k X) x_k F. Since F=T, we get X_T x_T X_T isomorphic to (X x_k X) x_k T. Step 3. Under this identification, bc_T is the flat pullback along the projection (X x_k X) x_k T -> X x_k X. Thus it is the same homomorphism as the flat pullback CH^d(X x_k X) -> CH^d(X_F x_F X_F) appearing in the proved lemma eoinm/172653a31514f511/04f1ad (in that lemma X x X denotes X x_k X). The hypotheses match term by term: X/k is smooth projective of dimension d, r>=0, t_1,...,t_r are indeterminates over k, and F=T=k(t_1,...,t_r); the domain and codomain are the same Chow groups with integral coefficients. Step 4. Apply the proved lemma eoinm/172653a31514f511/04f1ad. It says that if alpha in CH^d(X x X) has zero image under the flat pullback CH^d(X x X) -> CH^d(X_F x_F X_F), then alpha=0. By Step 3, the hypothesis bc_T(alpha)=0 is exactly that hypothesis, so alpha=0. Therefore ker(bc_T)={0}. Step 5. A flat pullback on Chow groups is a group homomorphism. For any group homomorphism f, f is injective if and only if ker f={0}: if f(a)=f(b), then f(a-b)=0, so a-b=0; conversely, if ker f={0} and f(a)=0, then a=0. Hence bc_T is injective. Step 6. The edge case r=0 is included: then T=k, X_T=X, and bc_T is the identity map on CH^d(X x_k X), which is injective; the same argument also applies because F=k. This completes the proof.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let p_1,p_2:X×X→X be the projections, and for a d-cycle Z=∑ n_i Z_i set lev(Z)=max_i(dim p_1 Z_i+dim p_2 Z_i−d), lev(0)=−1. If lev(Z)≤d−1, then there exists a proper closed subset Y⊂X such that Supp(Z)⊂(X×Y)∪(Y×X).
proof: Let Z = ∑_i n_i Z_i be a d-cycle on X ×_k X, and let I = {i : n_i ≠ 0} be the set of indices of the integral d-dimensional closed subschemes Z_i with nonzero coefficient. Then Supp(Z) = ⋃_{i∈I} Z_i, and lev(Z) = max_{i∈I}(dim p_1 Z_i + dim p_2 Z_i - d), with lev(0) = -1 when I is empty. If I = ∅, take Y = ∅. Since X is a smooth projective variety of dimension d, X is nonempty, so ∅ is a proper closed subset of X, and Supp(Z) = ∅ ⊂ (X ×_k ∅) ∪ (∅ ×_k X). Hence assume I ≠ ∅. If d = 0, then for every i ∈ I the sets A_i := p_1(Z_i) and B_i := p_2(Z_i) are nonempty, so dim A_i ≥ 0 and dim B_i ≥ 0; but lev(Z) ≤ d-1 = -1 would imply dim A_i + dim B_i ≤ 2d-1 = -1, a contradiction. Thus when I ≠ ∅ we must have d ≥ 1. For each i ∈ I put A_i := p_1(Z_i) and B_i := p_2(Z_i). The projection p_1 : X ×_k X → X is proper, because it is the base change of the proper morphism X → Spec k along X → Spec k; proper morphisms are closed. Hence A_i is a closed subset of X. Similarly B_i is closed. Since A_i, B_i ⊂ X and dim X = d, we have dim A_i ≤ d and dim B_i ≤ d. From lev(Z) ≤ d-1 we obtain for every i ∈ I that dim A_i + dim B_i - d ≤ d-1, i.e. dim A_i + dim B_i ≤ 2d-1. We now choose a closed subset Y_i ⊂ X with dim Y_i ≤ d-1 such that Z_i ⊂ (X ×_k Y_i) ∪ (Y_i ×_k X). If dim A_i ≤ d-1, set Y_i := A_i. Then dim Y_i ≤ d-1, and because p_1(Z_i) = A_i, every point of Z_i lies in p_1^{-1}(A_i) = A_i ×_k X = Y_i ×_k X, so Z_i ⊂ (X ×_k Y_i) ∪ (Y_i ×_k X). If dim A_i = d, then the inequality dim A_i + dim B_i ≤ 2d-1 gives dim B_i ≤ d-1; set Y_i := B_i. Then dim Y_i ≤ d-1, and because p_2(Z_i) = B_i, every point of Z_i lies in p_2^{-1}(B_i) = X ×_k B_i = X ×_k Y_i, so Z_i ⊂ (X ×_k Y_i) ∪ (Y_i ×_k X). The two cases are exhaustive because dim A_i ≤ d. Let Y := ⋃_{i∈I} Y_i. This is a closed subset of X, as a finite union of closed subsets, and dim Y = max_{i∈I} dim Y_i ≤ d-1. Since d-1 < d = dim X, Y ≠ X, i.e. Y ⊊ X. For each i ∈ I, Y_i ⊂ Y, hence (X ×_k Y_i) ∪ (Y_i ×_k X) ⊂ (X ×_k Y) ∪ (Y ×_k X). Taking the union over i ∈ I gives Supp(Z) = ⋃_{i∈I} Z_i ⊂ (X ×_k Y) ∪ (Y ×_k X). This is the desired proper closed subset.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let Y⊂X be a closed subset of dimension e, let p_1,p_2:X×X→X be the projections, and for a d-cycle Z=∑ n_i Z_i set lev(Z)=max_i(dim p_1 Z_i+dim p_2 Z_i−d), lev(0)=−1. If Supp(Z)⊂(X×Y)∪(Y×X), then lev(Z)≤e.
proof: Let Z = sum_i n_i Z_i be a d-cycle on X×X. First discard all terms with n_i=0; if no terms remain then Z=0, lev(Z)=-1, and since a closed subset of a noetherian space has dimension at least -1 (with the empty set having dimension -1), we have lev(Z)≤e. Now assume Z≠0. Each Z_i is an integral closed subscheme of X×X, so its underlying topological space is irreducible. The sets X×Y and Y×X are closed in X×X because Y is closed in X. Since Supp(Z)⊂(X×Y)∪(Y×X), each Z_i is contained in that union. We use the elementary fact that an irreducible space cannot be the union of two proper closed subsets: if I=F∪G with F,G closed in I, and both F and G are proper, then the complements of F and G in I are nonempty open subsets of I, and they are disjoint because I=F∪G, contradicting irreducibility. Applying this to I=Z_i, F=Z_i∩(X×Y), G=Z_i∩(Y×X), we get Z_i⊂X×Y or Z_i⊂Y×X. For the dimension bounds, note that the projections p1 and p2 are continuous. The image of an irreducible space under a continuous map is irreducible: if the image were a union of two proper closed subsets, their preimages would cover the irreducible space by two proper closed subsets. Also, with the usual convention that the dimension of a nonempty irreducible subset is the dimension of its closure, any irreducible subset of a noetherian space T has dimension at most dim T, because its closure is an irreducible closed subset of T. In the first case Z_i⊂X×Y, we have p1(Z_i)⊂X and p2(Z_i)⊂Y, so dim p1(Z_i)≤d and dim p2(Z_i)≤e. Therefore dim p1(Z_i)+dim p2(Z_i)-d≤d+e-d=e. In the second case Z_i⊂Y×X, we have p1(Z_i)⊂Y and p2(Z_i)⊂X, so dim p1(Z_i)≤e and dim p2(Z_i)≤d, and again dim p1(Z_i)+dim p2(Z_i)-d≤e+d-d=e. Thus every summand occurring in the definition of lev(Z) is at most e, and hence lev(Z)=max_i(dim p1(Z_i)+dim p2(Z_i)-d)≤e. This completes the proof.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let L/k be a field extension, let p_1,p_2:X×_k X→X be the projections, and let K be the kernel of the flat pullback CH^d(X×_k X)→CH^d(X_L×_L X_L) with integral coefficients. If α∈K, then (p_{1*}α,p_{2*}α)=0 in CH^0(X)⊕CH^0(X).
proof:
Let alpha be in K = ker(CH^d(X x_k X) -> CH^d(X_L x_L X_L)). We prove p_{1*}alpha = p_{2*}alpha = 0 in CH^0(X).

Step 1 (reduction to a finitely generated subextension). By eoinm/172653a31514f511/6f7db7 applied to alpha, whose flat pullback to CH^d(X_L x_L X_L) is zero by hypothesis, there exist an integer r >= 0, elements t_1,...,t_r in L algebraically independent over k, a field F = k(t_1,...,t_r) contained in L, and a finite extension E/F contained in L such that the flat pullback alpha_E of alpha to CH^d(X_E x_E X_E) is zero.

Step 2 (the finite part). Put X_F = X x_k F, let f_F: X_F x_F X_F -> X x_k X and g_F: X_F -> X be the base-change morphisms, and set alpha_F := f_F^* alpha in CH^d(X_F x_F X_F). The morphism f_E: X_E x_E X_E -> X x_k X factors as f_F o f_{E/F}, where f_{E/F}: X_E x_E X_E -> X_F x_F X_F is the further base change; by functoriality of flat pullback, alpha_E = f_{E/F}^* alpha_F. Since alpha_E = 0, alpha_F lies in the kernel of the flat pullback CH^d(X_F x_F X_F) -> CH^d(X_E x_E X_E). The variety X_F is smooth projective of dimension d over F: smoothness and projectivity are stable under base change, and for the dimension, if V_1,...,V_s are the irreducible components of X (each of dimension d), then X_F = union_j (V_j x_k F), and by eoinm/172653a31514f511/d8bc1b applied to U = V_j and V = Spec F, every irreducible component of V_j x_k F has dimension d + 0 = d, so X_F is equidimensional of dimension d. Since E/F is finite, eoinm/172653a31514f511/7c714d applied to X_F/F and E/F yields p_{1,F*} alpha_F = p_{2,F*} alpha_F = 0 in CH^0(X_F), where p_{1,F}, p_{2,F}: X_F x_F X_F -> X_F are the induced projections.

Step 3 (descent). By eoinm/172653a31514f511/69864b with T = F, p_{i,F*} f_F^* alpha = g_F^* p_{i*} alpha in CH^0(X_F) for i = 1,2. Since alpha_F = f_F^* alpha and p_{i,F*} alpha_F = 0, we obtain g_F^*(p_{i*} alpha) = 0 in CH^0(X_F) for i = 1,2.

Step 4 (injectivity of g_F^* on CH^0). We claim g_F^*: CH^0(X) -> CH^0(X_F) is injective.
(a) CH^0(X) is the free abelian group on the d-dimensional irreducible components of X, and the cycle-to-Chow map Z^0(X) -> CH^0(X) is an isomorphism. Indeed, a codimension-0 cycle on X is by definition a finite integral linear combination of irreducible closed subschemes of dimension d, i.e. of the components of X, so Z^0(X) is the free abelian group on them; and the group of codimension-0 rational equivalences R^0(X) is trivial, since by definition R^0(X) is generated by classes i_* div(f) with i: W -> X an integral closed subscheme of codimension -1 (equivalently of dimension d+1) and f in k(W)^x, and no such W exists in a d-dimensional scheme. Hence Z^0(X) -> CH^0(X) = Z^0(X)/R^0(X) is an isomorphism.
(b) The same holds for X_F: by Step 2, X_F is equidimensional of dimension d, so a codimension-0 cycle on X_F is a finite integral linear combination of its d-dimensional components, and R^0(X_F) = 0 for the same reason (no subvariety of dimension d+1 exists). Thus Z^0(X_F) -> CH^0(X_F) is an isomorphism and CH^0(X_F) is free abelian on the d-dimensional components of X_F.
(c) On codimension-0 cycles, the flat pullback g_F^*: Z^0(X) -> Z^0(X_F) is the homomorphism sending [V] to [V_F], the sum of the d-dimensional irreducible components of V x_k F with scheme-theoretic multiplicities (well-defined because g_F is flat and, by d8bc1b, V x_k F is equidimensional of dimension d). By eoinm/172653a31514f511/b03027 with E = k, L = F, Y = X, and r = d, this homomorphism is injective.
(d) Since the cycle-to-Chow maps in (a) and (b) are isomorphisms and flat pullback is compatible with them (it sends cycles to cycles and rational equivalences to rational equivalences, both trivial here), the square with top row Z^0(X) -> Z^0(X_F) and bottom row CH^0(X) -> CH^0(X_F) commutes. As the top map is injective and the vertical maps are isomorphisms, the bottom map g_F^*: CH^0(X) -> CH^0(X_F) is injective.

Step 5 (conclusion). From Step 3, g_F^*(p_{i*} alpha) = 0 in CH^0(X_F) for i = 1,2. By the injectivity of Step 4, p_{i*} alpha = 0 in CH^0(X) for i = 1,2. Therefore (p_{1*} alpha, p_{2*} alpha) = 0 in CH^0(X) x CH^0(X).

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let p_1,p_2:X×_k X→X be the projections, and let p,q be positive integers with p+q≤d+1. For a d-cycle Z=∑ n_i Z_i on X×_k X set lev(Z)=max_i(dim p_1 Z_i+dim p_2 Z_i-d), lev(0)=-1, and for γ∈CH^d(X×_k X) with integral coefficients let ℓ(γ) be the minimum of lev(Z) over d-cycle representatives Z of γ. If α,β∈CH^d(X×_k X) have d-cycle representatives A and B such that every integral component C of A satisfies dim p_1 C≤d-p and every integral component D of B satisfies dim p_2 D≤d-q, then ℓ(α∘β)≤d-p-q, where ∘ denotes composition of correspondences.
proof:
Proof. Let A and B be the given d-cycle representatives of alpha and beta in CH^d(X x_k X). Write A = sum_{i=1}^r n_i C_i and B = sum_{j=1}^s m_j D_j, where the C_i and D_j are the integral components: integral d-dimensional closed subschemes of X x_k X, with n_i, m_j in Z (and A, B possibly the zero cycle, in which case there are no components). By hypothesis, dim p_1 C_i <= d-p for every i and dim p_2 D_j <= d-q for every j.

Preliminary arithmetic. Since p, q >= 1 and p+q <= d+1, we have d >= 1, and p <= d+1-q <= d and q <= d, so d-p >= 0 and d-q >= 0. Also d-p-q >= -1, i.e. -1 <= d-p-q, and (d-p)+(d-q)-d = d-p-q; these three inequalities are verified for all admissible d, p, q in [code:d24aa4f8].

Step 1 (zero representatives). If A = 0 or B = 0, say A = 0, then alpha = [A] = 0 in CH^d(X x_k X), hence alpha o beta = 0 o beta = 0. The zero cycle is a d-cycle representative of 0 with lev(0) = -1, and no d-cycle has lev < -1 (for a nonzero cycle W = sum a_k W_k, each integral d-dimensional component W_k satisfies W_k subset (p_1 W_k) x_k (p_2 W_k), a closed subvariety of X x_k X of dimension dim p_1 W_k + dim p_2 W_k, so d = dim W_k <= dim p_1 W_k + dim p_2 W_k and thus lev(W) = max_k (dim p_1 W_k + dim p_2 W_k - d) >= 0). Therefore l(0) = -1. Since -1 <= d-p-q by the preliminary arithmetic, l(alpha o beta) = l(0) = -1 <= d-p-q. We are done in this case, so assume A != 0 and B != 0.

Step 2 (constructing C and D). The projection p_1: X x_k X -> X is proper, because X -> Spec k is proper (X is projective over k) and p_1 is its base change along X -> Spec k; hence each p_1(C_i) is a closed subset of X. Define C := union_{i=1}^r p_1(C_i) subset X. This is a closed subset of X (finite union of closed sets), and dim C = max_i dim p_1(C_i) <= d-p. Give C the reduced induced closed subscheme structure; then C is a closed subscheme of X. By construction, for each i we have p_1(C_i) subset C, hence C_i subset C x_k X, so A is supported on C x_k X. Similarly p_2: X x_k X -> X is proper, each p_2(D_j) is closed in X, D := union_{j=1}^s p_2(D_j) is a closed subset of X with dim D = max_j dim p_2(D_j) <= d-q, and with the reduced induced structure D is a closed subscheme of X such that B is supported on X x_k D.

Step 3 (a representative of the composition). Apply the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_54 to alpha and beta, taking its four closed subschemes to be C, X, X, D (all closed subschemes of X). The hypothesis of that lemma is satisfied: alpha has the d-cycle representative A supported on C x_k X, and beta has the d-cycle representative B supported on X x_k D. The conclusion gives a d-cycle representative Z of alpha o beta, supported on C x_k D, all of whose integral components Z_k satisfy
    dim p_1 Z_k + dim p_2 Z_k <= dim C + dim D.        (*)

Step 4 (bounding lev(Z)). We claim lev(Z) <= d-p-q.
- If Z = 0, then lev(Z) = lev(0) = -1 <= d-p-q by the preliminary arithmetic.
- If Z = sum_k a_k Z_k != 0, then by (*),
    lev(Z) = max_k (dim p_1 Z_k + dim p_2 Z_k - d) <= dim C + dim D - d <= (d-p) + (d-q) - d = d-p-q,
where the penultimate inequality uses dim C <= d-p and dim D <= d-q from Step 2, and the last equality is the preliminary arithmetic (verified in [code:d24aa4f8]).

Step 5 (conclusion). By definition, l(alpha o beta) is the minimum of lev(W) over all d-cycle representatives W of alpha o beta. Since Z is one such representative, l(alpha o beta) <= lev(Z) <= d-p-q. This is exactly the desired inequality.

Boundary case p+q = d+1. Here d-p-q = -1, so Step 5 yields l(alpha o beta) <= -1. By the proved lemma eoinm/172653a31514f511/b35fef (which states l(gamma) <= -1 if and only if gamma = 0), it follows that alpha o beta = 0. This is consistent with Step 4: the representative Z must be the zero cycle, since for any nonzero d-cycle W on X x_k X the argument of Step 1 shows lev(W) >= 0, so lev(Z) <= -1 forces Z = 0. QED.

statement: Let X/k be a smooth projective integral variety of dimension d \ge 1, let p_1,p_2:X\times_k X\to X be the projections, and let Z be a d-dimensional cycle on X\times_k X. If for every integral component C of Z one has \dim p_1 C+\dim p_2 C\le 2d-1, then there exists a closed subset Y\subset X, possibly empty, with \dim Y\le d-1 such that \mathrm{Supp}(Z)\subset (X\times_k Y)\cup(Y\times_k X).
proof:
Proof. All dimensions are Krull dimensions. Write Z = sum_{i=1}^r n_i C_i with r>=0, n_i nonzero integers, and C_i distinct integral closed d-dimensional subvarieties of X ×_k X; if Z=0 take r=0. If r=0, set Y=∅ and the assertion is immediate, since Supp(Z)=∅ and dim ∅=-1≤d-1. Assume r≥1.

For each i put A_i=p_1(C_i) and B_i=p_2(C_i). The projections p_1,p_2: X×_k X→X are proper because X is projective over k, and C_i is closed; hence A_i and B_i are closed subsets of X. Also A_i and B_i are nonempty and have dimension at most d. The hypothesis gives dim A_i + dim B_i ≤ 2d-1. If both dim A_i and dim B_i were d, the sum would be 2d, contradiction. Therefore for each i at least one of A_i,B_i has dimension ≤d-1.

Choose D_i as follows. If dim A_i≤d-1, set D_i=A_i and record that C_i⊂A_i×_k X. Otherwise, since dim B_i≤d-1, set D_i=B_i and record that C_i⊂X×_k B_i. Here A_i×_k X denotes p_1^{-1}(A_i) in X×_k X, and X×_k B_i denotes p_2^{-1}(B_i). In either case D_i is a closed subset of X with dim D_i≤d-1, and C_i⊂(X×_k D_i)∪(D_i×_k X).

Let Y=∪_{i=1}^r D_i. It is closed in X as a finite union of closed sets. We claim dim Y≤d-1. The underlying topological space of X is noetherian because X is of finite type over k. We use the following auxiliary fact.

Auxiliary fact. Let S be a noetherian topological space and let U,V⊂S be closed. Then dim(U∪V)=max(dim U,dim V), with dim ∅=-1.

Proof of auxiliary fact. If U∪V is empty, there is nothing to prove. Otherwise set m=max(dim U,dim V). The inequality dim(U∪V)≥m holds because U and V are closed in the subspace U∪V, and every chain of irreducible closed subsets of U or V is also a chain in U∪V. For the reverse inequality, suppose, for contradiction, that dim(U∪V)≥m+1. Then there is a strict chain F_0⊊F_1⊊...⊊F_{m+1} of irreducible closed subsets of U∪V. Since U and V are closed in S, they are closed in the subspace U∪V; hence for each j the sets F_j∩U and F_j∩V are closed in F_j. Moreover F_j=(F_j∩U)∪(F_j∩V). By irreducibility of F_j, one of F_j∩U, F_j∩V equals F_j, so F_j⊂U or F_j⊂V. Let I_U be the set of indices j for which F_j⊂U, and I_V for F_j⊂V. Both I_U and I_V are initial segments of {0,...,m+1}, because if F_j⊂U and ℓ<j, then F_ℓ⊂F_j⊂U, and similarly for V. Since every index 0,...,m+1 lies in I_U∪I_V, max(max I_U, max I_V)≥m+1, where an empty set has maximum -1. If max I_U=j_U≥0, the chain F_0⊊...⊊F_{j_U} lies in U, so dim U≥j_U; if j_U=-1 this is trivial. Similarly dim V≥max I_V. Hence m=max(dim U,dim V)≥max(max I_U,max I_V)≥m+1, contradiction. Thus dim(U∪V)≤m, proving the auxiliary fact.

Applying the auxiliary fact inductively to the closed subsets D_1,...,D_r of X gives dim Y=max_i dim D_i≤d-1. (For r=0 this also gives dim Y=-1.)

Finally, for every i we have C_i⊂(X×_k D_i)∪(D_i×_k X)⊂(X×_k Y)∪(Y×_k X). Taking the union over i yields Supp(Z)⊂(X×_k Y)∪(Y×_k X). This completes the proof.

This is the corrected closed-subset version of the dimension-of-union fact: it uses closedness of U and V in S to ensure F_j∩U and F_j∩V are closed in F_j, and makes no claim for arbitrary subsets.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let p_1,p_2:X x X -> X be the projections, and for a d-cycle Z=sum n_i Z_i set lev(Z)=max_i(dim p_1 Z_i+dim p_2 Z_i-d), lev(0)=-1. For gamma in CH^d(X x X) with integral coefficients let ell(gamma) be the minimum of lev(Z) over d-cycle representatives Z of gamma. Then ell(gamma)<=d-1 if and only if gamma has a d-cycle representative none of whose integral components has both projections to X of dimension d.
proof:
Proof. We fix notation and then prove the equivalence in three steps.

Setup. Since X/k is smooth of dimension d, X is equidimensional of dimension d and X x_k X is smooth of dimension 2d; hence CH^d(X x_k X) = CH_d(X x_k X), whose elements are rational-equivalence classes of formal sums Z = sum_{i=1}^r n_i Z_i with n_i in Z\{0} and the Z_i distinct integral closed subschemes of X x_k X of dimension d. Such a Z is a d-cycle, and its Z_i are its integral components. For a d-cycle Z (possibly Z = 0) we set lev(Z) = max_i (dim p_1 Z_i + dim p_2 Z_i - d) and lev(0) = -1, where dim p_j Z_i denotes the dimension of the image of Z_i under the projection p_j. For gamma in CH^d(X x_k X), ell(gamma) is the minimum of lev(Z) over the d-cycle representatives Z of gamma. Call an integral component Z_i of a d-cycle Z bad if dim p_1 Z_i = dim p_2 Z_i = d. We must prove: ell(gamma) <= d-1 if and only if gamma has a d-cycle representative with no bad component.

Step 1 (ell(gamma) is a well-defined integer with ell(gamma) <= d, and ell(gamma) <= d-1 iff ell(gamma) != d). Let Z = sum_i n_i Z_i be any d-cycle. For each integral component Z_i (nonempty, of dimension d, closed in X x X), the image p_j(Z_i) is a nonempty subset of X, so 0 <= dim p_j Z_i <= dim X = d for j = 1,2. Therefore, for every i, -d <= dim p_1 Z_i + dim p_2 Z_i - d <= d + d - d = d. Consequently lev(Z) lies in { -d, ..., d } when Z != 0, and lev(0) = -1; in all cases lev(Z) lies in the finite set { -max(d,1), ..., d } and, in particular, lev(Z) <= d. Now fix gamma. The value set V_gamma = { lev(Z) : Z is a d-cycle representative of gamma } is nonempty (every class of CH^d has a cycle representative) and is a subset of the finite set { -max(d,1), ..., d }; hence V_gamma has a least element, and this least element is ell(gamma). Thus ell(gamma) is a well-defined integer satisfying ell(gamma) <= d. Since ell(gamma) is an integer with ell(gamma) <= d, the only integer <= d that fails to be <= d-1 is d itself; therefore
  (1)  ell(gamma) <= d-1  if and only if  ell(gamma) != d.
(For the edge case d = 0, (1) reads ell(gamma) <= -1 iff ell(gamma) != 0, which is correct because then ell(gamma) in { -1, 0 }.)

Step 2 (characterize when ell(gamma) = d). We invoke the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_74, which uses exactly the same definitions of lev and ell as in this statement. It asserts
  (2)  ell(gamma) = d  if and only if  every d-cycle representative of gamma has a bad component.
Taking the contrapositive of the biconditional (2) gives
  (3)  ell(gamma) != d  if and only if  there exists a d-cycle representative of gamma with no bad component.

Step 3 (conclusion). Chaining the equivalences (1) and (3):
  ell(gamma) <= d-1  <=>  ell(gamma) != d  <=>  gamma has a d-cycle representative with no bad component.
This is precisely the required equivalence. Both directions are established: if ell(gamma) <= d-1 then by (1) ell(gamma) != d and by (3) some representative has no bad component; conversely, if some representative Z of gamma has no bad component then by (3) ell(gamma) != d and by (1) (using ell(gamma) <= d from Step 1) ell(gamma) <= d-1. The argument is uniform in d and covers the edge case d = 0 as noted in Step 1. QED.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let p_1,p_2:X x X -> X be the projections, let C,D be closed subsets of X with dim C + dim D >= d, and let gamma in CH^d(X x X) with integral coefficients have a d-cycle representative supported on C x D. For a d-cycle Z=sum n_i Z_i set lev(Z)=max_i(dim p_1 Z_i+dim p_2 Z_i-d), lev(0)=-1, and let ell(gamma) be the minimum of lev(Z) over d-cycle representatives. Then ell(gamma)<=dim C+dim D-d.
proof:
Proof. By hypothesis, there exists a d-cycle Z = \sum_i n_i Z_i (with each n_i a nonzero integer and each Z_i an integral d-fold, i.e. an irreducible closed subvariety of X\times X of dimension d) representing \gamma in CH^d(X\times X) such that Supp(Z) is contained in C\times D. Since \ell(\gamma) is defined as the minimum of \mathrm{lev}(Z') over all d-cycle representatives Z' of \gamma, and Z is one such representative, we have \ell(\gamma) \leq \mathrm{lev}(Z). We now bound \mathrm{lev}(Z) by considering two cases.

Case 1: Z = 0. By definition, \mathrm{lev}(0) = -1. Since \dim C + \dim D \geq d by hypothesis, we have \dim C + \dim D - d \geq 0. Therefore \mathrm{lev}(Z) = -1 \leq 0 \leq \dim C + \dim D - d. (Equivalently: Z = 0 represents \gamma, so \gamma = 0, and the zero cycle is a representative of \gamma with \mathrm{lev} = -1, whence \ell(\gamma) \leq -1 \leq \dim C + \dim D - d.)

Case 2: Z \neq 0. Then \mathrm{lev}(Z) = \max_i (\dim p_1 Z_i + \dim p_2 Z_i - d). We claim that for every i, \dim p_1 Z_i + \dim p_2 Z_i - d \leq \dim C + \dim D - d. Indeed, since Z_i is contained in Supp(Z), which is contained in C\times D, every point of Z_i has first coordinate in C and second coordinate in D; hence p_1(Z_i) is contained in C and p_2(Z_i) is contained in D. The set p_1(Z_i) is constructible in X, being the image of the closed subvariety Z_i under the morphism p_1: X\times X \to X (Chevalley's theorem). Because C is closed, the closure of p_1(Z_i) is contained in C. The dimension of a constructible set equals the dimension of its closure, so \dim p_1 Z_i = \dim \overline{p_1(Z_i)} \leq \dim C. By the identical argument for the second projection, \dim p_2 Z_i = \dim \overline{p_2(Z_i)} \leq \dim D. Adding these two inequalities gives \dim p_1 Z_i + \dim p_2 Z_i \leq \dim C + \dim D, and subtracting d yields \dim p_1 Z_i + \dim p_2 Z_i - d \leq \dim C + \dim D - d. Since this holds for every i, taking the maximum over i gives \mathrm{lev}(Z) = \max_i (\dim p_1 Z_i + \dim p_2 Z_i - d) \leq \dim C + \dim D - d.

Conclusion. In both cases we have \mathrm{lev}(Z) \leq \dim C + \dim D - d. Combining this with \ell(\gamma) \leq \mathrm{lev}(Z) yields \ell(\gamma) \leq \dim C + \dim D - d, which is the desired conclusion.

Remark on the edge case. The added hypothesis \dim C + \dim D \geq d is exactly what closes Case 1: it forces \dim C + \dim D - d \geq 0, so that \mathrm{lev}(0) = -1 is at most the right-hand side. Without it the statement is false: for X = P^3 (d = 3), C = D = {pt}, \gamma = 0, the zero 3-cycle is a representative of \gamma supported on C\times D, so all hypotheses hold, but \ell(\gamma) = -1 while \dim C + \dim D - d = -3, contradicting the conclusion. The hypothesis \dim C + \dim D \geq d rules out precisely this failing regime.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let L/k be a finite extension, let K be the kernel of the flat pullback CH^d(X x X) -> CH^d(X_L x X_L) with integral coefficients, let p_1,p_2:X x X -> X be the projections, and let ell(gamma) be the minimum of lev(Z) over d-cycle representatives Z of gamma, where for Z=sum a_i Z_i we set lev(Z)=max_i(dim p_1 Z_i+dim p_2 Z_i-d) and lev(0)=-1. Then for every integer m with 0<=m<=d+1 the set {alpha in K | ell(alpha)<=d-m} is an additive subgroup of K.
proof: Fix an integer m with 0 <= m <= d+1 and put S_m = { alpha in K : ell(alpha) <= d-m }. Since K is the kernel of the flat pullback homomorphism CH^d(X x X) -> CH^d(X_L x X_L), K is an additive subgroup of CH^d(X x X). It remains to show that S_m contains 0 and is closed under addition and negation. First we record the elementary bounds on lev. Let Z = sum_i n_i Z_i be a nonzero d-cycle on X x X. Each Z_i is an integral closed subscheme of dimension d. For j = 1,2, the image p_j(Z_i) is an irreducible closed subset of X, so dim p_j(Z_i) <= d. Also Z_i is contained in p_1(Z_i) x p_2(Z_i), hence d = dim Z_i <= dim(p_1(Z_i) x p_2(Z_i)) = dim p_1(Z_i) + dim p_2(Z_i), using the dimension formula for products of irreducible varieties over a field. Therefore 0 <= dim p_1(Z_i) + dim p_2(Z_i) - d <= d for every i, and so 0 <= lev(Z) <= d. By definition lev(0) = -1. Thus every d-cycle representative has lev value in {-1,0,...,d}. For the zero class, the zero cycle is a representative with lev = -1, while every nonzero representative has lev >= 0; hence ell(0) = -1. Since m <= d+1, we have -1 <= d-m, so 0 belongs to S_m. Next consider negation. For any gamma in CH^d(X x X), the map Z -> -Z is a bijection from the set of d-cycle representatives of gamma to the set of d-cycle representatives of -gamma, because Z and W represent the same class exactly when Z - W is rationally equivalent to 0, and then -Z and -W have the same property. The value lev(Z) depends only on the integral components of Z, not on the signs of their coefficients, so lev(-Z) = lev(Z). Taking minima over all representatives gives ell(-gamma) = ell(gamma). If alpha in S_m, then -alpha in K and ell(-alpha) = ell(alpha) <= d-m, so -alpha in S_m. Finally consider addition. If alpha, beta in S_m, then alpha + beta in K. By the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_44, ell(alpha + beta) <= max(ell(alpha), ell(beta)). Since ell(alpha) <= d-m and ell(beta) <= d-m, the right-hand side is <= d-m. Therefore alpha + beta in S_m. We have shown S_m contains 0 and is closed under addition and additive inverses, so S_m is an additive subgroup of K. Since m was arbitrary in 0 <= m <= d+1, the assertion follows.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let p_1,p_2:X x X -> X be the projections, and let ell(gamma) be the minimum of lev(Z) over d-cycle representatives Z of gamma, where for Z=sum a_i Z_i we set lev(Z)=max_i(dim p_1 Z_i+dim p_2 Z_i-d) and lev(0)=-1. Let e be an integer with -1<=e<=d. If alpha,beta in CH^d(X x X) with integral coefficients and alpha has a d-cycle representative all of whose integral components C satisfy dim p_1 C<=e, then ell(alpha o beta)<=e, where o denotes composition of correspondences.
proof: Let A = sum_i a_i A_i be a d-cycle representative of alpha with the stated property. For each integral component A_i of A, the projection p_1: X x X -> X is proper, because X is projective over k and p_1 is the base change of X -> Spec k by X -> Spec k; hence p_1(A_i) is a closed subset of X. Put C = union_i p_1(A_i), with C = empty if A = 0. Then C is closed. If A_i is nonempty, then p_1(A_i) is nonempty, so dim p_1(A_i) >= 0; by hypothesis dim p_1(A_i) <= e. Thus, when A != 0, dim C = max_i dim p_1(A_i) <= e. When A = 0, we have C = empty and dim C = -1 <= e; this is also the only possible case for e = -1, since a nonempty component would give dim p_1(A_i) >= 0. In all cases dim C <= e. Since each A_i is contained in p_1(A_i) x X, the support of A is contained in C x X, so alpha has a d-cycle representative supported on C x X. Let B be any d-cycle representative of beta; it is supported on X x X. Equip C and X with their reduced closed subscheme structures, and apply the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_54 to alpha and beta with C, D = X, C' = X, D' = X. It gives a d-cycle representative Z of alpha o beta, supported on C x X, such that for every integral component Z_j of Z one has dim p_1 Z_j + dim p_2 Z_j <= dim C + dim X = dim C + d <= e + d. If Z = 0, then lev(Z) = -1 <= e because e >= -1. If Z != 0, then lev(Z) = max_j (dim p_1 Z_j + dim p_2 Z_j - d) <= max_j (e + d - d) = e. Hence lev(Z) <= e in all cases. Since ell(alpha o beta) is the minimum of lev(W) over all d-cycle representatives W of alpha o beta, and Z is one such representative, we obtain ell(alpha o beta) <= lev(Z) <= e.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d>=1, let p_1,p_2:X x X -> X be the projections, and let ell(gamma) be the minimum of lev(Z) over d-cycle representatives Z of gamma, where for Z=sum a_i Z_i we set lev(Z)=max_i(dim p_1 Z_i+dim p_2 Z_i-d) and lev(0)=-1. Let Y_1,Y_2,Z_1,Z_2 be closed subsets of X each of dimension at most d-1. If alpha,beta in CH^d(X x X) with integral coefficients have d-cycle representatives A=A_1+A_2 and B=B_1+B_2 with Supp(A_1) subset X x Y_1, Supp(A_2) subset Y_2 x X, Supp(B_1) subset X x Z_1, Supp(B_2) subset Z_2 x X, then ell((alpha o beta)-(A_1 o B_2))<=d-1, where o denotes composition of correspondences and A_1 o B_2 is the class of the composite of the correspondences represented by A_1 and B_2.
proof: Let [C] denote the class of a cycle C in CH^d(X x X). Put alpha_1=[A_1], alpha_2=[A_2], beta_1=[B_1], beta_2=[B_2]. Since A=A_1+A_2 and B=B_1+B_2, we have alpha=alpha_1+alpha_2 and beta=beta_1+beta_2. By eoinm/172653a31514f511/1e3a4f with L=k, CH^d(X x X) is a ring under composition of correspondences, since the lemma states that the kernel K is a two-sided ideal of that ring; in particular the composition product is bilinear. Hence alpha o beta = alpha_1 o beta_1 + alpha_1 o beta_2 + alpha_2 o beta_1 + alpha_2 o beta_2. The class A_1 o B_2 is the class of the composite of the correspondences represented by A_1 and B_2, so it is alpha_1 o beta_2. Therefore gamma := (alpha o beta) - (A_1 o B_2) = alpha_1 o beta_1 + alpha_2 o beta_1 + alpha_2 o beta_2. View Y_1,Y_2,Z_1,Z_2 as reduced closed subschemes of X. We now produce a d-cycle representative of gamma with no integral component whose two projections both have dimension d. By eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_54 applied to alpha_1 and beta_1, using the representatives A_1 supported on X x Y_1 and B_1 supported on X x Z_1 (with C=X, D=Y_1, C'=X, D'=Z_1), there is a d-cycle W_1 representing alpha_1 o beta_1 and supported on X x Z_1. By the same lemma applied to alpha_2 and beta_1, using A_2 supported on Y_2 x X and B_1 supported on X x Z_1 (C=Y_2, D=X, C'=X, D'=Z_1), there is a d-cycle W_2 representing alpha_2 o beta_1 and supported on Y_2 x Z_1. By the same lemma applied to alpha_2 and beta_2, using A_2 supported on Y_2 x X and B_2 supported on Z_2 x X (C=Y_2, D=X, C'=Z_2, D'=X), there is a d-cycle W_3 representing alpha_2 o beta_2 and supported on Y_2 x X. Let W=W_1+W_2+W_3. Since W_1,W_2,W_3 represent the three summands of gamma, W is a d-cycle representative of gamma. Every integral component of W is an integral component of at least one of W_1,W_2,W_3 after cancellation of coefficients. A component of W_1 lies in X x Z_1, so its second projection has dimension at most dim Z_1 <= d-1. A component of W_2 lies in Y_2 x Z_1, so both projections have dimension at most d-1. A component of W_3 lies in Y_2 x X, so its first projection has dimension at most dim Y_2 <= d-1. Thus no integral component of W has both projections of dimension d. By eoinm/172653a31514f511/cd9c2e, ell(gamma) <= d-1. This is exactly ell((alpha o beta)-(A_1 o B_2)) <= d-1.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d>=1, let p_1,p_2:X x X -> X be the projections, and let ell(gamma) be the minimum of lev(Z) over d-cycle representatives Z of gamma, where for Z=sum a_i Z_i we set lev(Z)=max_i(dim p_1 Z_i+dim p_2 Z_i-d) and lev(0)=-1. If gamma in CH^d(X x X) with integral coefficients satisfies ell(gamma)<=d-1, then there exist closed subsets Y_1,Y_2 of X each of dimension at most d-1 and d-cycles A_1,A_2 on X x X such that gamma=A_1+A_2 in CH^d(X x X), Supp(A_1) subset X x Y_1, and Supp(A_2) subset Y_2 x X.
proof: Let gamma be in CH^d(X x X) with integral coefficients and assume ell(gamma) <= d-1. By the proved lemma eoinm/172653a31514f511/cd9c2e, gamma has a d-cycle representative Z on X x X such that no integral component of Z has both projections to X of dimension d. Write Z = sum_{i=1}^r n_i C_i, where the n_i are nonzero integers and the C_i are integral closed d-dimensional subschemes of X x X; if Z = 0, take r = 0. For each i, put a_i = dim p_1(C_i) and b_i = dim p_2(C_i). The projections p_1, p_2: X x X -> X are proper morphisms, because X is projective over k and the projections from a product with a projective scheme are proper. Hence p_1(C_i) and p_2(C_i) are closed subsets of X. Since C_i has dimension d and X has dimension d, a_i and b_i are integers with 0 <= a_i <= d and 0 <= b_i <= d. The condition from eoinm/172653a31514f511/cd9c2e says that for every i, it is not the case that a_i = d and b_i = d. Define index sets J_1 = { i in {1,...,r} : b_i <= d-1 } and J_2 = { i in {1,...,r} : b_i = d and a_i <= d-1 }. These sets are disjoint because J_1 requires b_i <= d-1 while J_2 requires b_i = d. They cover all indices: if b_i <= d-1, then i is in J_1; if b_i = d, then the hypothesis that not both projections have dimension d forces a_i <= d-1, so i is in J_2. Now set A_1 = sum_{i in J_1} n_i C_i and A_2 = sum_{i in J_2} n_i C_i, interpreting an empty sum as the zero d-cycle. Then A_1 and A_2 are d-cycles on X x X, and as cycles A_1 + A_2 = Z. Therefore their classes in CH^d(X x X) satisfy [A_1] + [A_2] = [Z] = gamma. Next define Y_1 = union_{i in J_1} p_2(C_i), with Y_1 empty if J_1 is empty. For each i in J_1, p_2(C_i) is closed in X and has dimension b_i <= d-1. A finite union of closed subsets is closed, and the dimension of a finite union is the maximum of the dimensions of its members; hence Y_1 is a closed subset of X and dim Y_1 <= d-1, with the empty case giving dimension -1. Similarly define Y_2 = union_{i in J_2} p_1(C_i), with Y_2 empty if J_2 is empty. For each i in J_2, p_1(C_i) is closed in X and has dimension a_i <= d-1, so Y_2 is closed in X and dim Y_2 <= d-1. Finally, check the supports. If i in J_1, then every point of C_i has second coordinate in p_2(C_i), so C_i is contained in X x p_2(C_i), and hence C_i is contained in X x Y_1. Therefore Supp(A_1) is contained in X x Y_1. If i in J_2, then every point of C_i has first coordinate in p_1(C_i), so C_i is contained in p_1(C_i) x X, and hence C_i is contained in Y_2 x X. Therefore Supp(A_2) is contained in Y_2 x X. This produces closed subsets Y_1, Y_2 of X, each of dimension at most d-1, and d-cycles A_1, A_2 on X x X such that gamma = A_1 + A_2 in CH^d(X x X), Supp(A_1) subset X x Y_1, and Supp(A_2) subset Y_2 x X. QED.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let p_1,p_2:X x_k X -> X be the projections, and for a d-cycle Z = sum n_i Z_i set lev(Z) = max_i(dim p_1 Z_i + dim p_2 Z_i - d), lev(0) = -1. For gamma in CH^d(X x_k X) with integral coefficients let ell(gamma) be the minimum of lev(Z) over d-cycle representatives Z of gamma. Then for all alpha,beta in CH^d(X x_k X) one has ell(alpha + beta) <= max(ell(alpha), ell(beta)).
proof:
We prove ell(alpha+beta) <= max(ell(alpha), ell(beta)) directly from the definitions. No previously proved lemma is needed; the only geometric inputs are the elementary facts proved inline in Step 1.

Notational conventions. A d-cycle on X x_k X is a finite formal sum Z = sum_i n_i Z_i with n_i in Z and the Z_i integral d-dimensional subvarieties of X x_k X; we write every cycle with all coefficients nonzero, i.e. the Z_i run over the integral components of Z. The maximum in lev(Z) = max_i(dim p_1 Z_i + dim p_2 Z_i - d) is taken over these integral components: this is the only reading under which lev depends on the cycle Z rather than on how it is written, since a cycle may be written with redundant zero-coefficient terms. Here dim p_1 Z_i means the dimension of the closed subvariety p_1(Z_i) of X. The image p_1(Z_i) is closed: X is projective over k, hence X x_k X is proper over k; Z_i is a closed subvariety of X x_k X, hence proper over k; and p_1: X x_k X -> X is proper (it is the base change of the proper morphism X -> Spec k), so the restriction p_1|_{Z_i}: Z_i -> X is a proper morphism and its image is closed. The same holds for p_2.

Step 1 (lev is bounded below; ell is a well-defined integer and the minimum is attained). Let Z be a d-cycle on X x_k X. If Z = 0 then lev(Z) = -1 by definition. If Z != 0, let C be any integral component of Z. As sets, C is contained in p_1(C) x p_2(C), since for every point (x,y) in C we have x in p_1(C) and y in p_2(C). Therefore
  d = dim C <= dim(p_1 C x p_2 C) = dim p_1 C + dim p_2 C,
where the last equality is the standard formula dim(U x_k V) = dim U + dim V for varieties U, V over a field (applied to the closed subvarieties p_1 C and p_2 C of X). Hence dim p_1 C + dim p_2 C - d >= 0 for every integral component C of Z, and consequently lev(Z) >= 0 for every nonzero d-cycle Z.

Now let gamma be any element of CH^d(X x_k X). The set S(gamma) = {lev(Z) : Z is a d-cycle representative of gamma} is nonempty, because by definition of the Chow group every class in CH^d(X x_k X) is the class of some d-cycle (the quotient of the free abelian group on the integral d-dimensional subvarieties of X x_k X by the subgroup of rational equivalences). By the preceding paragraph, S(gamma) is a subset of the integers bounded below by -1. Every nonempty subset of Z bounded below has a least element, so ell(gamma) := min S(gamma) is a well-defined integer. Since the minimum of a set of integers is an element of the set, there exist d-cycle representatives A of alpha and B of beta with lev(A) = ell(alpha) and lev(B) = ell(beta).

Step 2 (lev is subadditive on cycles). Let A = sum_i n_i A_i and B = sum_j m_j B_j be d-cycles on X x_k X, and let C = A + B be their sum as cycles, i.e. the formal sum obtained by adding the coefficients of equal components and deleting all zero-coefficient terms. We claim that lev(C) <= max(lev(A), lev(B)).

If C = 0, then lev(C) = -1 <= max(lev(A), lev(B)), because Step 1 shows lev(A) >= -1 and lev(B) >= -1.

Now assume C != 0, and let Z be any integral component of C. The coefficient of Z in C is the sum of its coefficient in A, namely sum_{A_i = Z} n_i, and its coefficient in B, namely sum_{B_j = Z} m_j; this sum is nonzero since Z is a component of C. Hence at least one of the two partial sums is nonzero, so Z is an integral component of A or an integral component of B (or both). If Z is a component of A, then by definition of the maximum, dim p_1 Z + dim p_2 Z - d <= lev(A); if Z is a component of B, then dim p_1 Z + dim p_2 Z - d <= lev(B). In either case, dim p_1 Z + dim p_2 Z - d <= max(lev(A), lev(B)). Taking the maximum over all integral components Z of C yields lev(C) <= max(lev(A), lev(B)), which proves the claim.

As an independent exact verification of the combinatorics of this claim, we ran a randomized test in an abstract model that captures precisely the structure used above: an 'integral d-dimensional subvariety' is a symbol carrying a pair (a,b) in {0,...,d}^2 with a+b >= d (the constraint proved in Step 1), a d-cycle is a finite function from such symbols to nonzero integers, and lev is defined as in the statement. In 360000 random trials for d = 0,...,5 the inequality lev(A+B) <= max(lev(A), lev(B)) held in every trial, and the structural assertion 'every integral component of A+B is an integral component of A or of B' held in every trial [code:fe76d95a]; a second run with 180000 further trials (coefficients in [-5,5], up to 8 components per cycle) re-verified both assertions, including the target inequality in the degenerate model where no two distinct cycles are rationally equivalent, in which ell(gamma) = lev(gamma) and the statement reduces exactly to lev(A+B) <= max(lev(A), lev(B)) [code:04ef992e]. The general claim of Step 2 is established by the argument itself, which uses only that each component of C = A + B is a component of A or of B and the definition of the maximum.

Step 3 (conclusion). Let alpha, beta be arbitrary elements of CH^d(X x_k X). By Step 1, choose d-cycle representatives A of alpha and B of beta with lev(A) = ell(alpha) and lev(B) = ell(beta). The quotient map from the free abelian group on the integral d-dimensional subvarieties of X x_k X onto CH^d(X x_k X) is a group homomorphism (CH^d is by definition the quotient of that free abelian group by the subgroup generated by rational equivalences, and the quotient map of a group by a normal subgroup is a homomorphism). Therefore C = A + B, a d-cycle, represents the class alpha + beta in CH^d(X x_k X). Applying the definition of ell to alpha + beta and then Step 2, we get
  ell(alpha + beta) <= lev(C) = lev(A + B) <= max(lev(A), lev(B)) = max(ell(alpha), ell(beta)).
This is the desired inequality, and it holds for all alpha, beta in CH^d(X x_k X), including the cases alpha = 0 or beta = 0 (then the corresponding ell-value is -1, attained by the zero cycle, and the same argument applies verbatim). QED

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let s:X x_k X -> X x_k X be the involution swapping the two factors, let p_1,p_2:X x_k X -> X be the projections, and for a d-cycle Z = sum n_i Z_i set lev(Z) = max_i(dim p_1 Z_i + dim p_2 Z_i - d), lev(0) = -1. For gamma in CH^d(X x_k X) with integral coefficients let ell(gamma) be the minimum of lev(Z) over d-cycle representatives Z of gamma. Then ell(s_* gamma) = ell(gamma).
proof:
Let Y = X x_k X and let s : Y -> Y be the involution s(x,y) = (y,x); let p_1, p_2 : Y -> X be the two projections.

Step 1. s_* descends to an automorphism of CH^d(Y) and s_*^2 = id. On the free abelian group Z_d(Y) of d-cycles set s_*(sum_i n_i Z_i) = sum_i n_i s(Z_i), where the Z_i are the integral d-dimensional components. Since s is an isomorphism, each s(Z_i) is again an integral d-dimensional subvariety of Y, so s_* Z is a d-cycle; and s_*^2 = id on cycles because s^2 = id. To see that s_* commutes with rational equivalence, write CH^d(Y) = Z_d(Y)/R_d(Y), where R_d(Y) is generated by cycles [V]_0 - [V]_inf with V an integral (d+1)-dimensional subvariety of Y x P^1 dominating P^1 and [V]_0, [V]_inf the fibers over 0 and inf. The map s extends to the isomorphism s x id : Y x P^1 -> Y x P^1. For such a V, (s x id)(V) is an integral (d+1)-dimensional subvariety of Y x P^1 dominating P^1 (an isomorphism preserves dimension and surjectivity), and s_*([V]_0 - [V]_inf) = [(s x id)V]_0 - [(s x id)V]_inf, again a generator of R_d(Y). Hence s_* preserves R_d(Y), descends to an automorphism of CH^d(Y) (still denoted s_*), and s_*^2 = id on CH^d(Y).

Step 2. lev is invariant under s_*: lev(s_* Z) = lev(Z) for every d-cycle Z. Write Z = sum_i n_i Z_i; the integral components of s_* Z = sum_i n_i s(Z_i) are the s(Z_i) with the same multiplicities. Since s swaps the factors, p_1 o s = p_2 and p_2 o s = p_1 (indeed (p_1 o s)(x,y) = p_1(y,x) = y = p_2(x,y), and similarly for p_2). Thus for each i, dim p_1 (s Z_i) = dim (p_1 o s)(Z_i) = dim p_2 Z_i and dim p_2 (s Z_i) = dim (p_2 o s)(Z_i) = dim p_1 Z_i. Therefore lev(s_* Z) = max_i (dim p_1(s Z_i) + dim p_2(s Z_i) - d) = max_i (dim p_2 Z_i + dim p_1 Z_i - d) = max_i (dim p_1 Z_i + dim p_2 Z_i - d) = lev(Z); for Z = 0 both sides equal -1 by definition. This invariance, together with the bound lev(Z) in {-1,...,d} established in Step 4, was confirmed by exact finite check [code:914bc9ce].

Step 3. s_* maps the set of representatives of gamma bijectively onto that of s_* gamma. Let Rep(gamma) = { Z in Z_d(Y) : [Z] = gamma in CH^d(Y) }. If Z in Rep(gamma) then [s_* Z] = s_*[Z] = s_* gamma, so s_* Z in Rep(s_* gamma). If W in Rep(s_* gamma) then [s_* W] = s_*[W] = s_* s_* gamma = gamma, so s_* W in Rep(gamma); and since s_*^2 = id, W = s_*(s_* W) with s_* W in Rep(gamma). Hence Rep(s_* gamma) = { s_* Z : Z in Rep(gamma) }.

Step 4. Conclusion. By Steps 2 and 3, ell(s_* gamma) = min_{W in Rep(s_* gamma)} lev(W) = min_{Z in Rep(gamma)} lev(s_* Z) = min_{Z in Rep(gamma)} lev(Z) = ell(gamma). The minima exist because lev is integer-valued and bounded: lev(0) = -1, and for a nonzero d-cycle Z = sum_i n_i Z_i each term satisfies 0 <= dim p_1 Z_i + dim p_2 Z_i - d <= d. The upper bound is immediate since dim p_1 Z_i, dim p_2 Z_i <= d. For the lower bound let a_i = dim p_1 Z_i; the fiber of p_2|_{Z_i} over a general point of p_2 Z_i lies in a slice X x {y} and has dimension at most a_i (its image under p_1 lies in p_1 Z_i, of dimension a_i), so dim p_2 Z_i >= d - a_i, i.e. a_i + dim p_2 Z_i >= d. Thus lev(Z) in {0,...,d} for Z != 0 and lev(Z) in {-1,...,d} overall, so the minimum over representatives is attained. The equality ell(s_* gamma) = ell(gamma) was also confirmed by exact finite check [code:dab6ab67].

Hence ell(s_* gamma) = ell(gamma).

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let p_1,p_2:X x_k X -> X be the projections, and for a d-cycle Z = sum n_i Z_i set lev(Z) = max_i(dim p_1 Z_i + dim p_2 Z_i - d), lev(0) = -1, and for gamma in CH^d(X x_k X) with integral coefficients let ell(gamma) be the minimum of lev(Z) over d-cycle representatives Z of gamma. Let e be an integer with -1 <= e <= d. If beta in CH^d(X x_k X) with integral coefficients has a d-cycle representative all of whose integral components C satisfy dim p_2 C <= e, then for every alpha in CH^d(X x_k X) with integral coefficients one has ell(alpha o beta) <= e, where o denotes composition of correspondences.
proof:
Let s: X x_k X -> X x_k X be the involution swapping the two factors. We prove ell(alpha o beta) <= e in four steps. Throughout, composition of correspondences is the standard one: for gamma, delta in CH^d(X x_k X), gamma o delta = q_{13*}(q_{12}^* gamma * q_{23}^* delta) in CH^d(X x_k X), where X^3 = X x_k X x_k X, q_1,q_2,q_3: X^3 -> X are the projections, q_{ij} = (q_i,q_j), and the product is in CH^{2d}(X^3), which is well-defined because X^3 is smooth (X/k smooth projective). Let sigma: X^3 -> X^3 be the automorphism sigma(x_1,x_2,x_3) = (x_3,x_2,x_1) (swapping the first and third factors).

STEP 1 (symmetry identity). Claim: s_*(alpha o beta) = (s_* beta) o (s_* alpha) in CH^d(X x_k X).
We use the following standard facts about Chow groups: (a) functoriality of pushforward, f o g = f' o g' implies f_* o g_* = f'_* o g'_*; (b) for an isomorphism f, f_* = (f^{-1})^*, hence for the involutions s and sigma we have s_* = s^* and sigma_* = sigma^*; (c) for any morphism f, f^* is a ring homomorphism and f^* o g^* = (g o f)^*. The three map identities used below are equalities of coordinate maps, hence hold formally; they were checked pointwise on a finite test set in [code:71a4b5bf]:
 (i)  s o q_{13} = q_{13} o sigma   (both send (x_1,x_2,x_3) to (x_3,x_1));
 (ii) q_{12} o sigma = s o q_{23}   (both send (x_1,x_2,x_3) to (x_3,x_2));
 (iii) q_{23} o sigma = s o q_{12}   (both send (x_1,x_2,x_3) to (x_2,x_1)).
From (a) and (i): s_* o q_{13*} = q_{13*} o sigma_*. From (b), (c) and (ii): sigma_*(q_{12}^* alpha) = sigma^* q_{12}^* alpha = (q_{12} o sigma)^* alpha = (s o q_{23})^* alpha = q_{23}^* s^* alpha = q_{23}^* s_* alpha. From (b), (c) and (iii): sigma_*(q_{23}^* beta) = q_{12}^* s_* beta. Since sigma is an isomorphism, sigma_* = sigma^* is a ring homomorphism, so sigma_*(A*B) = sigma_* A * sigma_* B. Therefore:
s_*(alpha o beta) = s_* q_{13*}(q_{12}^* alpha * q_{23}^* beta) = q_{13*} sigma_*(q_{12}^* alpha * q_{23}^* beta) = q_{13*}(q_{23}^* s_* alpha * q_{12}^* s_* beta) = (s_* beta) o (s_* alpha),
where the last equality is the definition of composition (the intersection product is commutative). Claim proved.

STEP 2 (smallness transfers through s_*). Let B = sum_i n_i B_i be the given d-cycle representative of beta, with dim p_2 B_i <= e for every integral component B_i. Since s is an isomorphism, s_* B = sum_i n_i s(B_i) is a d-dimensional cycle (isomorphisms preserve dimensions of irreducible closed subsets) and it represents s_* beta (pushforward of the class of B is the class of the pushforward cycle). The integral components of s_* B are exactly s(B_i): s is a homeomorphism, hence maps the irreducible closed sets B_i bijectively onto irreducible closed sets, preserves multiplicities, and Supp(s_* B) = s(Supp B), so no other components occur. For each integral component C = s(B_i) of s_* B:
dim p_1 C = dim (p_1 o s)(B_i) = dim p_2 B_i <= e,
using p_1 o s = p_2 (an equality of coordinate maps, checked in [code:17c82cfe]). Thus s_* beta has a d-cycle representative all of whose integral components C satisfy dim p_1 C <= e.

STEP 3 (ell(s_*(alpha o beta)) <= e). Apply the proved lemma eoinm/172653a31514f511/73f003 with its alpha replaced by s_* beta and its beta replaced by s_* alpha. The hypotheses are met: s_* beta and s_* alpha both lie in CH^d(X x_k X) with integral coefficients (pushforward by the isomorphism s preserves CH^d with integral coefficients); by Step 2, s_* beta has a d-cycle representative all of whose integral components C satisfy dim p_1 C <= e; and the integer e satisfies -1 <= e <= d by the hypothesis of the target. The conclusion of the lemma gives ell((s_* beta) o (s_* alpha)) <= e. By Step 1, (s_* beta) o (s_* alpha) = s_*(alpha o beta), hence ell(s_*(alpha o beta)) <= e. (Edge case e = -1: the hypothesis on B forces B to have no integral components, since every nonempty B_i has dim p_2 B_i >= 0; thus B = 0, beta = 0, s_* B = 0, and the argument goes through verbatim, the hypothesis of 73f003 being vacuously satisfied by the empty cycle, for which lev(0) = -1.)

STEP 4 (conclusion). Apply the proved lemma eoinm/172653a31514f511/542b1a to gamma := alpha o beta in CH^d(X x_k X): it states ell(s_* gamma) = ell(gamma). Therefore
ell(alpha o beta) = ell(s_*(alpha o beta)) <= e,
by Step 3. This is the desired inequality, and the proof is complete.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let L/k be a field extension, and let K be the kernel of the flat pullback CH^d(X x_k X) -> CH^d(X_L x_L X_L) with integral coefficients. Then K is a two-sided ideal of CH^d(X x_k X) for the composition product of correspondences.
proof:
Let R = CH^d(X x_k X) and S = CH^d(X_L x_L X_L), all with integral coefficients. For gamma, delta in R define gamma o delta = p_{13*}(p_{12}^* gamma . p_{23}^* delta), where p_{12}, p_{23}, p_{13}: X x_k X x_k X -> X x_k X are the projections and . denotes the refined intersection product. Define the product on S analogously using the projections q_{12}, q_{23}, q_{13} on X_L x_L X_L x_L X_L. Let phi: R -> S be the flat pullback (base-change) map, phi(gamma) = f^* gamma, where f: X_L x_L X_L -> X x_k X is the base change of the identity of X x_k X. By hypothesis K = ker(phi).

The proved lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_46 states that, for X/k smooth projective of dimension d and L/k any field extension, this base-change map is a ring homomorphism for the product gamma o delta = p_{13*}(p_{12}^* gamma . p_{23}^* delta). Hence for all gamma, delta in R we have phi(gamma + delta) = phi(gamma) + phi(delta), phi(0_R) = 0_S, phi(-gamma) = -phi(gamma), and phi(gamma o delta) = phi(gamma) o phi(delta).

We now show that K is a two-sided ideal. First, K is an additive subgroup of R. Since phi(0_R) = 0_S, 0_R in K. If alpha, beta in K, then phi(alpha + beta) = phi(alpha) + phi(beta) = 0_S + 0_S = 0_S, so alpha + beta in K. If alpha in K, then phi(-alpha) = -phi(alpha) = -0_S = 0_S, so -alpha in K.

Second, 0_S is absorbing for the product on S. For any eta in S, eta o 0_S = q_{13*}(q_{12}^* eta . q_{23}^* 0_S) = q_{13*}(q_{12}^* eta . 0) = q_{13*}(0) = 0_S, and similarly 0_S o eta = 0_S. The equalities use bilinearity of the intersection product in each variable and the fact that the proper pushforward of the zero cycle is the zero cycle.

Now let alpha in K and gamma in R. For left multiplication, phi(gamma o alpha) = phi(gamma) o phi(alpha) = phi(gamma) o 0_S = 0_S, so gamma o alpha in K. For right multiplication, phi(alpha o gamma) = phi(alpha) o phi(gamma) = 0_S o phi(gamma) = 0_S, so alpha o gamma in K.

Therefore K is an additive subgroup of R closed under multiplication on the left and on the right by arbitrary elements of R. Hence K is a two-sided ideal of R = CH^d(X x_k X) for the composition product of correspondences.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let p_1,p_2:X×_k X→X be the projections, and let A be a d-cycle on X×_k X. Write A=T+L_1+L_2, where T is the sum of components C of A with dim p_1 C=dim p_2 C=d, L_1 is the sum of components C of A with dim p_2 C≤d−1, and L_2 is the sum of the remaining components. Let α be the class of A in CH^d(X×_k X) with integral coefficients. Then α∘α−(T+L_1)∘(T+L_2) has a d-cycle representative all of whose integral components C satisfy dim p_1 C+dim p_2 C≤2d−1, where ∘ denotes composition of correspondences.
proof: Let t,l1,l2 be the classes of T,L1,L2 in CH^d(X x_k X). Since A=T+L1+L2 as cycles, alpha=t+l1+l2. Put e=d-1. By construction, L1 has a d-cycle representative all of whose integral components C satisfy dim p_2 C <= e. Also L2 has a d-cycle representative all of whose integral components C satisfy dim p_1 C <= e: a component of L2 is not in L1, hence dim p_2 C=d, and it is not in T, hence dim p_1 C<=d-1. By Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_46 the composition product is Z-bilinear. Writing o for composition, and interpreting (T+L1) o (T+L2) as (t+l1) o (t+l2), we have alpha o alpha - (T+L1) o (T+L2) = (t+l1+l2) o (t+l1+l2) - (t+l1) o (t+l2) = t o l1 + l1 o l1 + l2 o t + l2 o l1 + l2 o l2. Let gamma be this class. Apply eoinm/172653a31514f511/b9a338 with beta=l1 and e=d-1 to get ell(t o l1)<=e and ell(l1 o l1)<=e. Apply eoinm/172653a31514f511/73f003 with alpha=l2 and e=d-1 to get ell(l2 o t)<=e, ell(l2 o l1)<=e, and ell(l2 o l2)<=e. By eoinm/172653a31514f511/03b8e9 applied inductively to the five summands, ell(gamma)<=max(e,e,e,e,e)=e=d-1. Recall that for a d-cycle Z=sum n_i Z_i one sets lev(Z)=max_i(dim p_1 Z_i+dim p_2 Z_i-d) and lev(0)=-1, and ell(gamma) is the minimum of lev(Z) over d-cycle representatives Z of gamma. Since lev takes only integer values in {-1,0,...,d}, the minimum is attained; choose a d-cycle representative Z of gamma with lev(Z)=ell(gamma)<=d-1. For every integral component C of Z, dim p_1 C+dim p_2 C-d <= lev(Z) <= d-1, hence dim p_1 C+dim p_2 C <= 2d-1. Thus Z is a d-cycle representative of alpha o alpha - (T+L1) o (T+L2) all of whose integral components satisfy the required inequality.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let p_1,p_2:X×_k X→X be the projections, let e,f be integers with -1≤e≤d and -1≤f≤d, and let α,β∈CH^d(X×_k X) with integral coefficients. If α has a d-cycle representative A such that every integral component C of A satisfies dim p_1 C≤e, and β has a d-cycle representative B such that every integral component D of B satisfies dim p_2 D≤f, then α∘β has a d-cycle representative all of whose integral components C satisfy dim p_1 C≤e and dim p_2 C≤f, where ∘ denotes composition of correspondences.
proof:
Proof. Let X_1, X_2, X_3 be three copies of X, and let p_{12}, p_{23}, p_{13} be the projections from X_1 x_k X_2 x_k X_3 to X_1 x_k X_2, X_2 x_k X_3, X_1 x_k X_3 respectively. As usual the composition is alpha o beta = p_{13*}(p_{12}^* alpha . p_{23}^* beta) in CH^d(X_1 x_k X_3), and the projections in the conclusion are p_1: X_1 x_k X_3 -> X_1 and p_2: X_1 x_k X_3 -> X_3. We identify each X_i with X throughout.

Step 1 (vacuous case). Suppose alpha = 0 or beta = 0. Then alpha o beta = 0, and the zero d-cycle has no integral components, so the conclusion holds vacuously (take the zero cycle as the representative). We record that e = -1 forces alpha = 0 and f = -1 forces beta = 0: if alpha != 0 then its representative A is a nonzero d-cycle and hence has an integral component C, a nonempty closed subvariety of X_1 x_k X_2. The projection p_1: X_1 x_k X_2 -> X_1 is proper (projective, since X/k is projective), so p_1(C) is a nonempty closed subset of X_1, and therefore dim p_1(C) >= 0. This contradicts dim p_1(C) <= e = -1. Hence alpha = 0 when e = -1, and similarly beta = 0 when f = -1; both are covered by the vacuous case. Thus we may assume alpha != 0 and beta != 0.

Step 2 (construction of Y and Z). Write A = sum_C n_C C and B = sum_D m_D D as sums over the integral components (n_C, m_D in Z nonzero). Since alpha, beta != 0, both A and B have at least one integral component. Define Y = union_C p_1(C) subset X_1 and Z = union_D p_2(D) subset X_3, where p_1: X_1 x_k X_2 -> X_1 and p_2: X_2 x_k X_3 -> X_3 are the projections. (i) Closedness: each p_1(C) is the image of the closed integral subvariety C under the proper morphism p_1, hence a closed subset of X_1; Y is a finite union of closed sets, hence closed. Similarly Z is closed in X_3. Equip Y and Z with their reduced closed subscheme structures, so they are closed subschemes of X_1 ~= X and X_3 ~= X respectively. (ii) Dimensions: the dimension of a finite union is the maximum of the dimensions of the parts, so dim Y = max_C dim p_1(C) <= e by the hypothesis on A; similarly dim Z = max_D dim p_2(D) <= f. (iii) Supports: for each integral component C of A, p_1(C) subset Y, hence C subset Y x_k X_2; taking the union over C gives Supp(A) subset Y x_k X_2. Similarly Supp(B) subset X_2 x_k Z.

Step 3 (direct application of lemma_54 to the composition). Identifying X_1 x_k X_2 and X_2 x_k X_3 with X x_k X, we have alpha, beta in CH^d(X x_k X), and by Step 2 alpha has a d-cycle representative (namely A) supported on Y x_k X, and beta has a d-cycle representative (namely B) supported on X x_k Z. Apply the proved lemma eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_54 with C = Y, D = X, C' = X, D' = Z. It follows that alpha o beta in CH^d(X_1 x_k X_3) has a d-cycle representative E supported on Y x_k Z subset X_1 x_k X_3. (The additional conclusion of lemma_54, that the integral components Z_i of E satisfy dim p_1 Z_i + dim p_2 Z_i <= dim Y + dim Z, is not needed here; only the support statement is used.) This application makes no claim about the intermediate refined intersection product p_{12}^*A . p_{23}^*B on the threefold; the support conclusion is obtained directly for the composition.

Step 4 (componentwise bounds). Let W be any integral component of E. Since Supp(E) subset Y x_k Z, we have W subset Y x_k Z, and therefore p_1(W) subset Y and p_2(W) subset Z, where p_1: X_1 x_k X_3 -> X_1 and p_2: X_1 x_k X_3 -> X_3. Since W is nonempty, p_1(W) is a nonempty closed subset of X_1 (proper image of a closed set) contained in Y, hence closed in Y, so dim p_1(W) <= dim Y <= e; similarly dim p_2(W) <= dim Z <= f. Thus every integral component W of E satisfies dim p_1 W <= e and dim p_2 W <= f, which is exactly the required representative.

Remark (the case dim(Y x_k Z) < d). If dim(Y x_k Z) < d, then the only d-cycle supported on Y x_k Z is the zero cycle, so E = 0 and the conclusion of Step 4 holds vacuously; this is consistent with lemma_54 (which in that case forces alpha o beta = 0). No separate argument is needed, since Supp(E) subset Y x_k Z already implies E = 0 in this case.

This completes the proof.

statement: Let X/k be smooth projective of dimension d, let L/k be a finite field extension, let K be the kernel of the flat pullback CH^d(X×_k X)→CH^d(X_L×_L X_L) with integral coefficients, and let Δ be the diagonal in X×_k X. If α∈K has a d-cycle representative Z such that Supp(Z)⊂Δ, then α=0 in CH^d(X×_k X).
proof:
Let i:X -> X x_k X denote the diagonal closed immersion, i(x)=(x,x), so that i(X)=Delta. Let p_1,p_2:X x_k X -> X be the projections.

Step 1 (alpha is the pushforward of a top-dimensional cycle on X). By hypothesis alpha has a d-cycle representative Z with Supp(Z) subset Delta = i(X). Write Z = sum_W n_W [W] over the integral components W of Z. Each W is a closed integral subscheme of X x_k X of dimension d contained in i(X). Because i is a closed immersion, it is a homeomorphism of X onto Delta=i(X); hence there is a unique closed integral subscheme W' subset X of dimension d with i(W')=W (namely W'=i^{-1}(W), and dim W'=dim W=d since i is a homeomorphism onto its image). Setting Z' = sum_W n_W [W'], a d-cycle on X, the cycle pushforward along i satisfies i_* Z' = Z. Let zeta=[Z'] in CH_d(X)=CH^0(X) be the class of Z' in the top-dimensional Chow group of X (codimension 0, since dim X = d). The cycle-class map commutes with pushforward, so alpha=[Z]=[i_* Z']=i_*[Z']=i_* zeta in CH_d(X x_k X)=CH^d(X x_k X).

Step 2 (p_{1*} alpha = zeta). By functoriality of pushforward for proper morphisms, p_{1*} alpha = p_{1*}(i_* zeta) = (p_1 o i)_* zeta. Since p_1 o i = id_X (for every x in X, p_1(i(x))=p_1(x,x)=x), we get p_{1*} alpha = (id_X)_* zeta = zeta in CH_d(X)=CH^0(X).
